documented_patterns_on_the_page.title: When a deal ended or changed, the company sued the state
documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary: Foreign companies that bought or ran privatized water, gas and power services, or held mining rights, have used investment treaties to sue governments that froze tariffs, changed contracts, took services back or stopped a deal, including when protests forced it. Most of these claims went to ICSID, the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes in Washington, which its own website calls "one of the five organizations of the World Bank Group". The legal basis was usually a bilateral investment treaty, an agreement between two countries that lets a company from one sue the other.

Of these foreign roles, 140 (81%) belong to companies based in today's high-income countries and 96 (55%) to companies based in the G7 (the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Canada, Italy, Germany and Japan). documented_patterns_on_the_page.title: Aid money that goes back to companies in the donor country
documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary:
Tied aid is aid that must be spent on goods or services from the country that gave it. Eurodad, a European network of groups working on debt and aid, counted about $26.9 billion of tied aid in 2018, or 21% of bilateral and EU aid. Its total for formal and informal tying together is at least $32.3 billion and possibly up to $37.9 billion. It puts the direct short-term cost of tying at $2 billion to $7 billion.

documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary: Two studies measure aid against UN politics. documented_patterns_on_the_page.title: Funds that buy old debt and sue in New York and London
documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary:
When a country cannot pay, most lenders usually accept a reduced deal. A holdout refuses and sues for the full amount. A vulture fund is the critics' name for a fund that buys defaulted debt to do this. An ECB working paper (no. 2135, 2018) by Schumacher, Trebesch and Enderlein counted 158 cases against 34 defaulting governments from 1976 to 2010: 130 in US courts (82.3%), 23 in the UK (14.6%) and 5 in arbitration. New York law governs almost half of outstanding sovereign bonds (White & Case, 2024) or over 50% (Insurance Journal, 2026).

documented_patterns_on_the_page.title: Debt relief: the Paris Club, China and who goes first
documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary: The Paris Club is an informal group of creditor governments, dating to 1956, that reschedules loans together, case by case and tied to an IMF-backed programme. Lex Rieffel, a former US Treasury desk officer for it, writes that "China, however, is not a member," and lists it among ad hoc participants. He cites a study by Horn, Reinhart and Trebesch putting debt owed to China at $370 billion at end-2017, against $246 billion owed to the 22 Paris Club members. documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary:
Foreign direct investment earns income for its owners, and part stays in the host country. Globally in 2011, nearly one-third stayed in host economies and two-thirds went back to investors.

documented_patterns_on_the_page.title: Investment routed through tax havens, and the tax that goes missing
documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary: UNCTAD said in 2015 that about 30% of cross-border corporate investment passes through offshore hubs, and estimated developing countries lose about $100 billion a year in tax on investment linked to those hubs. Across developing economies, each 10 percentage points of offshore investment goes with a 1-point lower rate of return. IMF economists Damgaard, Elkjaer and Johannesen wrote in 2019 that phantom investment, money passing through empty companies, comes to $15 trillion, almost 40% of global FDI, up from about 30% less than a decade earlier. hyps.title: Forecasts inflated so countries borrow more
hyps.conviction: An insider's account, the World Bank's own 1992 review, a 245-dam study and an IMF working paper all find forecasts biased upward. Whether the bias is deliberate is the suspicion.
story: In 1971 a young economist named John Perkins went to work for Chas. T. Main, an engineering firm in Boston, and by his own account rose to be its chief economist. In a 2004 book, Confessions of an Economic Hit Man, he wrote that his real job had been to produce inflated growth forecasts, so that countries would take large loans for power and infrastructure projects built by US companies and be left owing more than they could pay. Critics disputed many of his claims, above all that the National Security Agency was involved in hiring him. Einar Greve, the vice-president who hired him, at first backed the book's general account and later denied parts of it, including any link to the NSA. The suspicion this entry describes does not depend on Perkins: it is that the forecasts behind big loans are pushed upward on purpose, costs written low and benefits written high, so the loan gets approved and the contractors get paid, and the borrowing country carries the debt when the numbers never arrive.

The World Bank's own review points the same way. In 1992 its Wapenhans report found that 37.5 per cent of the Bank's projects completed in 1991 were judged failures, up from 15 per cent in 1981. It blamed an "approval culture" in which staff treated project appraisals as a way to win approval, and found a growing bias toward over-optimistic expected returns.

So do other studies. In 2014 an Oxford team, Atif Ansar, Bent Flyvbjerg and colleagues, studied 245 large dams in 65 countries built between 1934 and 2007. On average the dams cost 96 per cent more than budgeted, three in four ran over, and Ansar told International Rivers that dams backed by development banks did no better. The study names deliberate underestimating to win approval as one of the root causes. In 2020 an IMF working paper found the Fund's own growth forecasts too optimistic by about 0.2 percentage points a year, adding up to about one point over five years, and more optimistic the deeper the budget cuts the programme planned. On this map, the Yacyretá dam between Paraguay and Argentina saw its cost rise from $2.5 billion to over $10.5 billion, or over $15 billion by International Rivers' count.

An honest mistake and a deliberate one leave the same trace in a forecast, so the missing piece is intent. It would show in the working files: appraisal models and consultants' forecasts for large loan-financed projects, read beside the drafts they replaced and the outcomes that followed. The World Bank's evaluation office says the inside history of the 1992 task force is documented in the Bank's archives, and a count of how often forecasts were raised under deadline pressure would test whether the bias was pushed or simply drifted.
hyps.missing: No study has compared draft and final appraisal forecasts across the Bank's portfolio.
hyps.would_settle: Appraisal models and consultant forecasts for large loan-financed projects, compared draft against final and against outcomes, starting from the Portfolio Management Task Force files in the World Bank archives.

countries.note: Central to Perkins's book, which claims President Jaime Roldós was killed for opposing the country's creditors.

hyps.title: Rescue loans that rescue the banks, not the country
hyps.conviction: Leaked IMF board minutes and a line-by-line study of where the Greek money went. Whether rescues are designed this way as a rule is the suspicion.
story: On 9 May 2010 the IMF's board met in Washington to approve its share of a €110 billion rescue for Greece, behind minutes marked strictly confidential. When they reached the Wall Street Journal in 2013, they showed Brazil's director warning that the programme might be seen not as a rescue of Greece but as a bailout of Greece's private debt holders, mainly European financial institutions, and directors for Argentina, Brazil, India, Russia and Switzerland saying it lacked any cut in Greece's debt to private lenders. The Dutch, French and German directors told the board their banks would broadly keep their Greek bonds; according to The Press Project, banks from those three countries held more than $122 billion of them early in 2010 and began selling that spring. A 2016 study by the European School of Management and Technology in Berlin found that of €215.9 billion paid out in Greece's first two programmes, less than 5 per cent went into the Greek budget for anything other than old debts, interest and bank rescues, though its authors also blamed years of high Greek spending. On this map, the 2012 Greek programme cut the minimum wage by 22 per cent, and other cards record the protests that followed. The suspicion is that big rescue loans are designed first to pay foreign private lenders back in full, moving their losses onto the borrowing country's taxpayers, while the country gets years of cuts.

Mexico in 1995 had the same shape. In 1994 the Mexican government had sold short-term bonds called tesobonos, paid in pesos but tied to the value of the dollar, and the amount outstanding grew from $3.1 billion in March to $29.2 billion in December, about $17 billion of it held by foreign investors. When the peso collapsed that December, the United States put together a rescue of about $50 billion, including $20 billion from the US Treasury and $17.8 billion from the IMF, which let Mexico pay the bonds as they fell due. Critics in Washington called it a bailout of Wall Street investors in Mexican bonds. Mexico repaid the US loans early, with interest, and the Clinton administration called it a success.

In Mexico the bondholders were paid what they were owed, and the public lenders who replaced them were then repaid by Mexico. Who held the bonds at the moment of each rescue is rarely published, which is what makes it hard to say whose losses were avoided.

What would settle the question are the full IMF staff papers behind the 2010 Greek programme, the European Central Bank's records of which Greek bonds it bought and from whom, the month-by-month exposure reports of the named banks in 2010, and a list of who held Mexico's tesobonos in January 1995. Together they would show whether these rescues were shaped around getting particular creditors out before the losses fell.
hyps.missing: The ECB's bond-purchase counterparty records and month-by-month bank exposure data for 2010 have not been obtained.
hyps.would_settle: Full IMF staff papers for the 2010 Greek arrangement; ECB records of Greek bond purchases by counterparty; month-by-month 2010 exposure reports of the French, German and Dutch banks.

hyps.title: Secret loans arranged by banks and traders, kept from the public
hyps.conviction: A bank's guilty plea, debts revealed overnight in Congo and Chad, and $385 billion of underreported Chinese-linked debt. That hidden lending is routine is the suspicion.
story: In the port of Maputo, Mozambique, a fleet of tuna boats bought with borrowed money has sat rusting for years. In 2013 and 2014 three companies linked to Mozambique's state borrowed about $2 billion through Credit Suisse and Russia's VTB for the fleet and for coastal security, and the loans were taken without the approval of Mozambique's parliament, with more than $1 billion of them kept secret from the IMF until 2016. The Financial Times reported that the deals had been inflated from $300 million to over $2 billion. US authorities said about $200 million went in bribes and kickbacks, about $150 million of it to Mozambican officials and about $50 million to Credit Suisse bankers. In 2021 Credit Suisse admitted fraud, agreed to pay about $475 million to US and UK authorities, and cancelled $200 million of Mozambique's debt. A study by Mozambique's Centre for Public Integrity and Norway's Chr. Michelsen Institute put the cost to the economy at $11 billion and found the slowdown pushed nearly two million people into poverty. The suspicion is that this is not unusual: that arranging hidden loans is ordinary business for some international banks and commodity traders, and that the public finds out only when the country can no longer pay.

Commodity traders make hidden loans too. In the Republic of Congo, Glencore and Trafigura had lent the government money to be repaid in future oil. In 2017 the IMF raised its estimate of Congo's debt from 77 to 110 per cent of national income after hidden debts came to light; Debt Justice said it could not tell how much of the jump was hidden debt and how much was falling output or new loans. Global Witness later found the state oil company carrying up to $3.3 billion more that had never been disclosed. In Chad, Glencore held 98 per cent of the government's foreign commercial debt by the end of 2016, and in 2016 $231 million of the government's $271 million in net oil revenue, about 85 per cent, went to Glencore.

The same thing happens with Chinese lending and in Europe. In 2021 AidData found about $385 billion of debt linked to Chinese lending that poorer governments had not reported, mostly because it was owed by state companies and special-purpose firms rather than the government itself. In Europe, Goldman Sachs arranged currency swaps for Greece in 2001 that hid about €2.8 billion of debt, after Greece had joined the euro; Goldman said the swaps were legal under the rules of the time.

These debts stay hidden because the World Bank's debt register relies on what governments choose to report, loans to state companies are often left out, and trader prepayment deals are private contracts. AidData found the size of the gap for Chinese lending by comparing what lenders recorded with what borrowers reported. Nobody has done the same for Western banks and commodity traders, and doing so country by country would show how much of the world's debt is missing from the official numbers.
hyps.missing: No creditor-side comparison has been made for Western banks and commodity traders as AidData did for Chinese lenders.
hyps.would_settle: A country-by-country comparison of creditor-side records (bank and trader filings, BIS data) with debtor reports to the World Bank Debtor Reporting System.

hyps.title: Poor countries chosen to take rich countries' toxic waste
hyps.conviction: A World Bank memo set out the logic and a commodity trader's ship followed it. Whether waste flows follow that logic as a rule is the suspicion.
story: On the night of 19 August 2006, lorries began dumping black liquid at rubbish tips and roadsides around Abidjan, the largest city in Côte d'Ivoire. It was more than 500 tonnes of waste from the Probo Koala, a ship chartered by the oil trader Trafigura, which had tried to unload it in Amsterdam that July and taken it back on board. In Abidjan a newly licensed local firm, Compagnie Tommy, was hired to get rid of it for about $17,000. More than 100,000 people sought medical help; a national inquiry recorded 15 deaths and an Ivorian court 17. Trafigura paid the government about $198 million in 2007 in a settlement that ended prosecution, and £30 million in 2009 to about 30,000 people who had sued in London, both without admitting liability, and a Dutch court fined it €1 million in 2010 for concealing how dangerous the waste was. Trafigura has always said the waste could not have caused deaths or serious injury. The suspicion is that companies, and some of the economists who advise the big lenders, treat people in poor countries as cheaper to poison, and that hazardous waste travels to where harming people costs least.

The logic had been written down at the World Bank. A memo dated 12 December 1991 went out under the name of Lawrence Summers, then the Bank's chief economist. It argued that health-damaging pollution should be done where its cost was lowest, which meant the country with the lowest wages, and it called the economic logic of dumping a load of toxic waste in the lowest-wage country "impeccable". The memo was actually written by a Bank economist, Lant Pritchett. Both men said it was meant as sarcasm, and Pritchett said the leaked version had been doctored to remove context. Friends of the Earth leaked it in February 1992 to the Brazilian newspaper Jornal do Brasil, and Brazil's environment secretary, José Lutzenberger, replied that the reasoning was logical and insane.

The trade it describes has a long record. In 1987 and 1988 two Italian firms arranged to store about 18,000 drums of hazardous waste in the Nigerian port of Koko, paying a local man about $100 a month for the use of his yard; the drums leaked, Nigeria forced Italy to take them back, and the scandal helped bring about the Basel Convention on hazardous waste in 1989. When China stopped accepting plastic waste for recycling at the start of 2018, exports from rich countries moved to Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia, where illegal plants burned plastic in the open; Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines later shipped containers of contaminated waste back to the countries that had sent them.

Shipments like these are often hidden by calling waste something else, such as a ship's slops, building materials or goods for recycling. Countries that have signed the Basel Convention report their exports each year. Matching those reports against the wages and the waste-treatment capacity of the countries receiving the waste would show whether the trade follows the memo's logic or not.
hyps.missing: No analysis matching Basel Convention export reports to destination wages and treatment capacity.
hyps.would_settle: Basel Convention national reports on hazardous waste exports, matched to destination-country wages and treatment capacity.

hyps.title: Loans cut off to bring down governments the West dislikes
hyps.conviction: Declassified notes, congressional records and freedom-of-information documents show lending stopped for political reasons in Chile, Nicaragua and Haiti. That this is a standing weapon is the suspicion.
story: On 15 September 1970, eleven days after Salvador Allende won Chile's presidential election, President Richard Nixon met the CIA's director, Richard Helms, in the White House. Helms's handwritten notes of the meeting, declassified in 1975 during a Senate investigation, include the instruction to make the economy scream. In the years that followed, the World Bank made no new loans to Chile, and the Senate investigation found that loans from the Inter-American Development Bank fell from $46 million in 1970 to $2 million in 1972. After the 1973 coup that brought General Augusto Pinochet to power, World Bank loans flowed again. Historians still argue over how much the cut-off itself hurt Chile, since the IMF kept lending and some older loans kept paying out. The suspicion is that cutting off lending through the banks the West controls is a standing weapon, used to weaken governments the United States dislikes, in ways voters in the target country never see as a decision.

Nicaragua in the 1980s is the second case. After the Sandinistas came to power, the United States opposed their loan requests at the World Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank. In January 1985 the US Secretary of State, George Shultz, wrote to the president of the Inter-American Development Bank warning against a proposed $58 million loan to Nicaragua and raising future US funding for the bank. Several of the bank's member governments criticized the letter at the bank's annual meeting that March, and the Heritage Foundation reported that the bank approved no new loans for Nicaragua after 1983.

Haiti in 2001 is the third. The Inter-American Development Bank had approved four loans worth $146 million for health, drinking water, roads and education in Haiti between 1996 and 1998. After Jean-Bertrand Aristide's party won elections in 2000, the money was not paid out. On 6 April 2001 the US executive director at the bank, Lawrence Harrington, wrote to its president asking that the loans not be paid out, and the Robert F. Kennedy Memorial Center, which later obtained Treasury documents through freedom-of-information requests and a lawsuit, says the bank's about-face followed. A 2003 Congressional Research Service report also listed disputes over the 2000 elections, Haiti's arrears to the bank and unmet loan conditions as reasons the money was held up. Haiti's water system went without the money while the bank, according to press reports, still asked Haiti to pay arrears; in July 2003 Haiti paid $32 million to clear them, leaving about $3 million in its reserves.

Most of what passes between the US Treasury and its directors at the development banks is never published, and the RFK Center had to go to court to get some of it. What would settle the question is the full set of US instructions to its directors on loans to governments it opposed, and a count of how often approved or pending loans stalled after elections the United States did not like.
hyps.missing: No count of loans stalled after elections the US opposed; Treasury instructions to its directors largely unreleased.
hyps.would_settle: US Treasury instructions to its executive directors at the World Bank and IDB on loans to governments it opposed, and a count of stalled loans after disfavoured election results.

hyps.title: Aid money used to win arms sales
hyps.conviction: A British court ruled aid for Malaysia's Pergau dam unlawful amid a linked arms deal, and BAE paid Tanzania £29.5 million after an overpriced military radar sale. That aid budgets are bent to sell weapons is the suspicion.
story: On 10 November 1994 the High Court in London ruled that the British government had acted unlawfully when it gave £234 million of aid to build the Pergau dam in Malaysia. The case was brought by the campaign group World Development Movement, which argued the dam was so uneconomic that it could not count as development. Behind it lay an arms deal: Margaret Thatcher had promised help with the dam in 1989 while Britain was negotiating a £1.3 billion sale of weapons to Malaysia, and officials told a parliamentary committee that the arms deal would have been lost without the aid promise. The suspicion is that aid budgets are regularly bent to win weapons and other large contracts for the donor country's companies, so that money given in the name of the poor ends up paying for deals that serve the donor's industry.

Tanzania shows the other direction of the same trade. In a deal agreed in 1999 and cleared for export by Britain in 2001, the British arms company BAE Systems sold Tanzania, one of the world's poorest countries and a large recipient of British aid, a military radar system for about £28 million to use for civil air traffic control. The World Bank and the International Civil Aviation Organization said it was too expensive and unsuited to the job, and Britain's development secretary, Clare Short, delayed a £10 million aid payment and suggested the deal was corrupt. Investigators later found that BAE had paid about $12 million to a marketing adviser; the case never established where the money went after that. In 2010 BAE pleaded guilty in Britain only to an accounting offence and agreed to pay £29.5 million, which was paid in 2012 for textbooks and other school supplies in Tanzania.

The radar deal came to court only through a fraud investigation, and the 2010 plea agreement ended it with an accounting offence, so the bribery allegations were never tested at trial. The same aid ministries that give money to poor countries sit inside governments that promote their own arms and engineering exporters, and the record of how those interests are weighed against each other is rarely published.

What would settle how common this is are the internal files linking aid offers to export deals in donor governments, starting with the ones released in Britain's own Pergau inquiry, and a count, donor by donor, of how often large aid packages coincided with arms or major equipment sales to the same country.
hyps.missing: No donor-by-donor count of large aid packages coinciding with arms or major equipment sales.
hyps.would_settle: Donor government files linking aid offers to export deals; a count of large aid packages coinciding with arms sales to the same country.

hyps.title: Pension funds and university endowments behind land grabs
hyps.conviction: In a preliminary report, Brazil's land agency found that land deals involving a US pension manager broke limits on foreign ownership, and a Brazilian court froze the deed to land held by Harvard's endowment; research groups link the farms to land grabbing and deforestation. That ordinary people's savings are financing land grabs worldwide is the suspicion.
story: In the Matopiba region of Brazil's Cerrado, the world's most biodiverse savannah, some of the farms that took over land from traditional communities after 2008 were bought with the retirement savings of American university teachers and with Harvard University's endowment. Research by the Brazilian network Rede Social and the group GRAIN found that Harvard's endowment had spent more than $1 billion over a decade on about 850,000 hectares of farmland on five continents, nearly 300,000 hectares of it in the Cerrado, while Chain Reaction Research reported that the pension manager TIAA had bought at least 13 farms in Matopiba, at least four from companies associated with a man known in the region for illegal land grabbing. Both funds have been linked to deforestation and fires on their land. In a preliminary report revealed in December 2020, Brazil's land agency, Incra, found that TIAA's indirect part in land bought by a Brazilian company it co-owns broke Brazil's limits on foreign land ownership, which TIAA disputes; in October 2020 a Bahia state court froze the deed to a 107,000-hectare tract held by Harvard's Brazilian company and reopened an inquiry into whether it was public land illegally transferred to private hands. The suspicion is that the savings of ordinary people in rich countries, held by pension funds and endowments, are financing land grabs and forest clearing across the world, out of sight of the people whose money it is.

The rush began after the financial crash of 2008, when pension funds, endowments and private equity looked for assets that would hold their value, and farmland was one. In 2015 GRAIN and Rede Social reported that Sweden's national pension fund AP2 and two Canadian pension funds, the Caisse de dépôt et placement du Québec and British Columbia's bcIMC, had put money into a global farmland fund that bought Brazilian farms through a structure of companies and debentures which, the groups said, let them evade Brazil's limits on foreign land ownership; the fund's manager said the farms were bought legally. In parts of the Cerrado, GRAIN reports, false land titles are commonly used to claim public land before it is sold on.

The funds say they apply strict standards and that some problems predate their purchases. But the savers and institutions whose money pays for these farms are generally not told which farms they own, and the corporate layers make it hard even for researchers to know.

What would settle how far this reaches is a full list of the farmland held by the largest pension funds and endowments, by country and by farm, checked against land registries, deforestation maps and records of evictions. Such lists exist inside the funds and are not published.
hyps.missing: No public farm-level list of pension fund and endowment farmland holdings.
hyps.would_settle: Farm-level farmland holdings of the largest pension funds and endowments, checked against land registries, deforestation data and eviction records.

hyps.title: Big investment funds that refuse debt relief and profit from the crisis
hyps.conviction: The World Bank records that only one private creditor joined the G20's 2020 debt suspension; Zambia's bondholders refused relief while government lenders gave it. That large funds deliberately hold out to profit from poor countries' crises is the suspicion.
story: In September 2020 Zambia, hit by the pandemic, asked all its lenders to let it pause payments for six months. Government lenders, including China, agreed to suspend about $600 million. Holders of Zambia's $3 billion of international bonds refused, and on 13 November 2020, after missing a $42.5 million interest payment, Zambia became the first African country to default in the pandemic. The largest known bondholder was BlackRock, the world's biggest asset manager, with about $220 million of the bonds. The campaign group Debt Justice estimated that BlackRock had paid about $165 million for them and could make 110 per cent profit if paid in full; BlackRock disputed this and said it was likely to make losses when its bonds matured. Zambia's 2021 budget gave more to debt payments than to education, health, water and sanitation combined. The bondholders agreed a deal only in 2024, which Debt Justice calculated still repaid them more than Zambia's government lenders received. The suspicion is that the large funds that now hold much of poor countries' debt use their position to refuse or delay relief, collect high interest while countries cut spending, and let governments and public lenders absorb the losses.

The pattern showed across the whole pandemic. In 2020 the G20 offered the poorest countries a pause in debt payments, the Debt Service Suspension Initiative, and encouraged private lenders to join. The World Bank recorded that it suspended $12.9 billion of payments between May 2020 and December 2021, and that only one private creditor took part. In 2020 no payments to private lenders were suspended under the scheme, while payments to governments were.

In 2023 Debt Justice calculated that private lenders holding the bonds of Ethiopia, Ghana, Sri Lanka, Suriname and Zambia could make $20 billion in profit if paid in full on bonds bought when issued, and $30 billion on bonds bought at the low prices of that time. The five countries' bonds are governed by English law (57 per cent) or New York law (43 per cent). Britain passed a law in 2010 that stops creditors claiming more in its courts than an earlier debt relief scheme allowed; campaigners have asked for it to be updated to cover current relief. BlackRock says it has a duty to its own clients, many of them saving for retirement, and cannot forgive sovereign debt on its own. This map's entry on hedge funds that buy debt cheap and sue shows the harder end of the same business.

What would settle it is the record of what each large fund paid for the bonds of countries that later sought relief, what it was finally paid, and what positions it took in the negotiations, set beside the relief given by public lenders. The bondholder committees' negotiating records are private, which is where the decision to hold out would show.
hyps.missing: No public record of each fund's purchase price, final recovery and negotiating position in recent restructurings.
hyps.would_settle: Purchase prices and final recoveries of the major bondholders in recent sovereign restructurings, with their negotiating positions, set against relief given by public lenders.

hyps.title: Credit ratings that punish poor countries for seeking debt relief
hyps.conviction: Rating agencies downgraded Ethiopia for applying to the G20's debt relief scheme; a UNDP study puts the cost of subjective ratings to 19 African countries at $74.5 billion; S&P and Moody's paid over $2 billion over inflated ratings for paying clients. That the agencies systematically protect private creditors at poor countries' expense is the suspicion.
story: On 29 January 2021 Ethiopia announced that it would ask for debt relief under the G20's new Common Framework, the scheme rich governments had set up so the poorest countries could restructure what they owed. On 9 February Fitch cut Ethiopia's rating from B to CCC, saying the request explicitly raised the risk of default. In March Moody's put Ethiopia on review for a downgrade, because the framework would require it to seek similar relief from private lenders, and in May it cut Ethiopia to Caa1. S&P also downgraded. Ethiopia's bonds fell, making any future borrowing dearer. The economist Jayati Ghosh wrote that governments would now fear entering talks with private creditors even within programmes designed to help them. Three firms, S&P, Moody's and Fitch, issue more than 90 per cent of outstanding credit ratings. The suspicion is that these agencies judge poor countries, and African ones above all, more harshly than the facts justify, and punish governments that try to cut their debts, in ways that protect the private investors who are their main audience while raising the cost of borrowing for the countries.

In 2023 the UN Development Programme studied the ratings of African countries. It estimated that if ratings were based on less subjective judgements, 19 African countries could save up to $74.5 billion in excess interest and lost lending, more than the continent receives in aid each year. Hippolyte Fofack, chief economist of the African Export-Import Bank, wrote in 2021 that more than half of rated African countries were downgraded in 2020, against a global average of 31.8 per cent. UNDP said the costs could arise from thin data and subjective methods rather than conscious bias, and its study found the agencies use similar methods worldwide.

The two largest agencies have paid to settle claims over inflated ratings. In 2015 S&P paid $1.375 billion and in 2017 Moody's paid about $864 million to settle US federal and state claims over their ratings of mortgage securities before the 2008 crash. Connecticut's attorney general said the states had alleged that Moody's ratings were influenced by the demands of the banks that issued the securities and paid for the ratings. Both firms accepted statements of facts and neither admitted breaking the law. The African Development Bank's president has called for Africa to have its own credit rating agency.

What would settle it is a full comparison of how the agencies rate African and other poor countries against richer countries with the same debt, growth and repayment record, and of every downgrade that followed a request for debt relief, with the agencies' internal committee notes. Those notes are not published.
hyps.missing: No published comparison of ratings for poor and rich countries with matching fundamentals; rating committee notes are private.
hyps.would_settle: Rating committee records and a matched comparison of ratings for poor versus richer countries with similar fundamentals, including all downgrades following debt-relief requests.

hyps.title: Foreign companies behind the overthrow of governments
hyps.conviction: Declassified CIA histories confirm the 1953 Iran coup followed the nationalisation of a British oil company and the 1954 Guatemala coup followed land reform against United Fruit; a US Senate inquiry found ITT offered the CIA $1 million against Allende. That companies with large investments still help remove governments that threaten them is the suspicion.
story: In 1952 Guatemala's elected president, Jacobo Árbenz, passed a land reform, Decree 900, that took uncultivated land from large estates and gave it to landless farmers. The biggest landowner was the American United Fruit Company, which held a large share of the country's farmland and left most of it unplanted. The government took hundreds of thousands of acres of the company's idle land and offered compensation based on the value United Fruit itself had declared for tax. The company lobbied Washington and spread the claim that Árbenz was a communist. In June 1954 a small force led by Carlos Castillo Armas invaded from Honduras, organised and armed by the CIA in an operation it called PBSUCCESS, and Árbenz resigned; Castillo Armas cancelled the land reform and returned the land to United Fruit. The CIA's own history of the operation, written in the 1990s, was later declassified. Some historians say the US acted mainly out of fear of communism and that there is no proof United Fruit organised the coup. The suspicion is that large foreign companies have repeatedly helped bring down governments that threatened their investments, using their own governments' spy agencies to do it, and that this has not stopped.

Iran's coup had come a year earlier. In May 1951 Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh nationalised the British-owned Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, the forerunner of BP. In August 1953 he was overthrown. In 2013 the CIA released an internal history stating that the coup was carried out under CIA direction as an act of US foreign policy, with British help; it also showed the CIA arranging $5 million for the new government within days. Britain has never officially acknowledged its part, and British officials in the 1970s tried to stop the US releasing documents that would embarrass the UK.

In Chile, a 1973 US Senate subcommittee on multinational corporations found that the American telephone company ITT, which feared that Salvador Allende would nationalise its Chilean company, had offered the CIA $1 million in 1970 to help stop him becoming president. The offer was turned down, while the CIA ran its own operations against Allende. In 1978 two ITT officials were charged with lying to the Senate about the company's actions in Chile; in 1979 the government dropped the case against one of them, Robert Berrellez, saying a trial would expose national security information. This map's entry on loans cut off to bring down governments tells what the US government did to Chile's lending at the same time.

These cases came out decades later, through congressional inquiries and declassified files. What would settle whether companies still play this part are the intelligence and foreign-ministry records of more recent coups and attempted coups in countries with large foreign investments, and the lobbying records of the companies involved, many of which remain classified or private.
hyps.missing: Few declassified records on company involvement in coups after the 1970s.
hyps.would_settle: Declassified intelligence and foreign-ministry records, plus company lobbying records, for recent coups and attempts in countries with large foreign investments.
